newsitem.title: INDIA: India needs $100 bln investment in power by 2002.
newsitem.headline: India needs $100 bln investment in power by 2002.

text.p: India's private power policy is aimed at attracting foreign investors who are expected to contribute a large chunk of the $100 billion needed to boost electricity output in the next five years, a senior government official said on Wednesday.

"The private power policy of the government of India has been formulated to adequately address the issues related to foreign private investment in the sector," Power Minister S. Venugopalachari told a seminar on the "Commercialisation fo State Electricity Boards".

Venugopalachari said though 86 percent of villages had access to electricity and a project to link various power regions to form a national grid was underway, the country continued to face acute shortages.

"In spite of the sizeable growth of the sector, the per capita consumption in the country continues to be quite low and the transmission and distribution losses are quite high coupled with low capacity utilisation," he said.
"The country currently faces shortages of about seven percent in energy and 17 percent in peaking power."
He said the demand for electricity was estimated to grow at an average eight percent annually, implying the need for an additional capacity of 10,000 MW every year for the next decade.
"The government is encouraging private sector investment in the power sector not only for conventional coal/gas-based plants but also hydro plants in a big way," Venugopalachari said.
"For the ninth plan period (1997-2002) it has been estimated that the country would require about $100 billion for the power sector," he said.
He said a large amount of the funds would have to be from foreign investment and the government had tailored its private investment policy to encourage these fund flows.

"The policy besides allowing an investor-friendly and market-driven tariff regime, also provides upto 100 percent protection against exchange rate fluctuations for foreign equity participants, the minister said.
He said proposals were also on the anvil to introduce legally enforceable fuel supply and fuel transport agreements which investors could enter into with the railways and coal companies.
The state-run Coal India, which has a monopoly to supply these services, gives no guarantee of regular supplies.
The government announced a Common Minimum National Action Plan for Power last December which recognised the widening demand-supply gap and outlined reforms needed in the sector.
"The plan lays adequate stress on restructuring of the state electricity boards (SEBs), rationalisation of retail tariff structure and autonomy to the SEBs ," he said.
